entries.title: TAKEOFF!!
entries.text: After one last good cup of tea we are on the road! My bag is a little lighter than expected but that’s not a problem, they made all the clothes in China anyway so can get more if needs be. My friend Will who works in the airport joined me for some pints on the layover  and the plane is ready for takeoff. Maybe 12 other non Chinese on the flight from all around the world. See you on the other side 🇨🇳😎

entries.title: Happy China National Day/ Dad Birthday/ Solo Day
entries.text:
Pretty cool so far! National day doesn’t have much public celebrations here in Chongqing which is a shame. Border security wasn’t too tough. I need to get an urgent lesson in Chinese tones as I’m clearly unintelligible 😭.

Shoutout to the chef who came out of the kitchen to teach me to eat noodles the Chinese way and his whole family for good vibes and conversation even if it was in Mandarin. Aymon arrives tomorrow which is when the party really starts🛬🎉

Happy birthday to Dad as well as China! Who knew!

entries.title: Chongqing, China
entries.text:
Aymon touched down on a beautiful Chongqing day. We really saw the multilayered nature of the city though it’s hard to capture in photos. No one knows where the real ground is.

Saw the biggest crane ever and it was on a boat! 

Are some mysterious street goop, not bad.

The wholesale shops here are insane. This glasses one went on a long way with different shops.

entries.title: We love Chongqing
entries.text: Texting in from a gorgeous high speed train through countryside that looks like a fairytale (pics attached, phone aperture too slow). Last day in Chongqing was awesome, Buddhist temple in the middle of skyscrapers was the highlight. Took the metro for a while to see the outskirts but the city just keeps going, skyscraper flats for tens of kilometres! Took the metro through an apartment block to start a series of things An Bord Pleanála would never allow alongside today’s train station.

entries.title: All China Village Basketball Championship
entries.text:
Insane 24 hours:

- Xinjiang Turpan won the All China Village Basketball Championship! We have been avid supporters since yesterday and will visit the town later

- This village is very small and only has the basketball once a year going on. Everyone thinks we’re from Xinjiang, either asking us or telling each other we are which is a fun surprise. Having great fun telling them I’m from Ireland, or when they don’t know Ireland (80% of the time) then Australia. It appears that many people here have never seen a foreigner before and are very very curious. There’s no such thing as walking past a group of people drinking here as they make you join them.

- Got taken in by some local kids and their grandmother to have lunch in their house in this TINY village, played basketball with the whole village. Their parents work in Guanzhou and don’t come home but left a BMW there, the kids have a real MacBook and watch brain rot on it but grow their own food.  Miao people are very friendly and kind

- Aymon was interviewed for something we don’t know what

- The show around the basketball was wild. One million Chinese flags. So many  performances. CCP notable deaths played to rave music. I can’t upload videos here but there is lots of strange things to share. Some pics attached.

- Miao people do eat dog :(

- We came back to middle aged people drinking in and around our room, one speaks English very well. They want to bring us to a similar football championship tomorrow, confirmation pending.

entries.title: All China International Football Tournament
entries.text:
We followed the middle aged crew from the night before to the All China International Football Tournament and it was awesome.

This was similar to the basketball with a team from every province AND 5 “village teams” from a few countries that are just random local teams that heard about it and asked to come. In a complete upset the best Chinese provincial level football team is… a random town in Brazil!!!!! 🇧🇷 These guys are not semi-professional or anything!!

We jumped the barriers and celebrated with the Brazilians, had moonshine rice liquor with the Malaysian delegation on the pitch, and afterwards were mistaken by everyone including the organisers as part of the Brazil team in some capacity and given winners garlands. 

This led to even more photos with random Chinese spectators to the extent that I was signing balls and we were brought into photos with actual team mates and locals. Brazil guys were great craic. We even saw 3 other foreigners there that weren’t playing, friends of the Australian on the Guangzhou team who the commentators just call “the Australian” 

12/10 experience highly recommend to everyone, including anyone with a half decent football team as the Malaysians (who were not a football team at all, they are the workers at a football academy and lost every game) were very very very well taken care of on their trip.

entries.title: Salaam Alaykum,
entries.text:
Salaam Alaykum,

For better or for worse, I havent been reading anything of what Matthew
(now knows as Ling Ling) has posted. This will either be an identical copy
of his work, and if not, it'll provide you with further insight into our
journey so far.

1. Matthew has surprisingly picked up Mandarin very quickly.

This is mostly due to him:
1. Nodding at the right time
2. Learning the chinese versions of (hmmm, oooohhh, woahhh)
3. Being very good at repeating back the last word of any sentence, having
no clue what he's repeating

This alone makes everyone assume he's fluent.

On top of this, Matthew has actually learnt some core Chinese vocab, seen
below (in chronological order):
• (No) meat
• Buddhist
• Xinjiang person
• Dog meat
• 2 metres

That provides a good summary of 80% of our interactions with the locals so
far.

2. The highlights of our trip so far as undoubtedly (and unsurprisingly)
been interactions with the locals

This ranges from:
• Kids in Taipan (basketball village) inviting us to their house for lunch,
followed by a basketball with all 7 children in the village
• A chinese Catholic priest (crazy in itself) opening the church so we
could see inside
• A masseuse (who we only found after asking this lovely lady at a
convenience store where to get a chinese massage), gifting us a ridiculous
amount of tea, undoubtedly way more expensive than what we paid him for the
foot massage
• Celebrating the Brasilian team winning the soccer tournament with a
Nigerian teammate (unsure how he's on the brasilian team) and the Malaysian
team
• Running into a British guy that was on the same flight as Matthew a week
ago, and helping him order his first hot meal in days (he's vegetarian,
with no chinese, and very scared)
• And the list goes on...

3. Tomorrow marks our last day in a big city

The day after, we'll be on a 48hr train taking us to the sticks of
Xinjiang.

After almost a week exploring Guizhou, it felt odd seeing foreigners today
for the first time in days. Americans in the convenience stores, English
tour groups in the temples, over-dressed Italians complaining about the
food. It's been a bit of a shock. Saying that, Chengdu has been a great
place to reset and chill with our new British mate.

Tuesday onwards, we have little clue what to expect.

• Will they even speak Chinese? Or will we need to learn Uyghur?
• Can we even use wechat pay? For context, in the last week the only times
we've had trouble with wechat pay was with Xinjiang vendors, and the
Church's gift shop. That's quite an *interesting* combination considering
where we are right now
• How many hotels actually accept foreigners?
• How will the locals feel towards foreigners?
• Will there be other foreigners?

I'm sure with more research we'd realistically have pretty good answers to
these questions. But what's the fun in that?

Worst comes to worst, we just get back on the train and beeline it to Xian,
so we're really not too concerned.

That's all for now, ciao ciao from Chengdu!

entries.title: Pre-train update
entries.text:
Very cool but less crazy Chinese stuff lately. Went to a real rice field, old villages, many temples in Guiyang and Chengdu. We have also been visiting the Catholic Churches of China as they are super cool and a mix of traditions, though our cards were declined in the gift shop strangely…

Met some cool people along the way and spent some time at the Chengdu bead convention which is apparently very big business. Aymon had zero luck at the marriage market but hopes remain high. The train begins tomorrow. Anticipation building. We have been informed there are no chargers or food onboard for our 3 day journey so we will prep as we can.

entries.title: Train Day 1
entries.text:
Day 1. 

We are set up in two middle bunks, friendly carriage mates. Full train. Spirits high. 

Supplies:

entries.title: Train Day 2
entries.text:
Not a terrible night. Train lights out at 22:00 and back on at 7:00. The grandmas are up and chatting loudly some time before that. We fell asleep in the jungle of South China and have awoken on Mars. The land of the Gansu Corridor is semi arid and desert in alternating parts. At points all we can see are pylons in all directions as far as the eye can see. Much of the train has taken pictures with us. 
Our new Chinese grandmothers are part of a group of 37 who travel together, they are returning to Xinjiang for the 7th time and have much to recommend. The rest of the train has worked in oil in the Taklamakan  Desert.
Claustrophobia at a minimum and spirits still high. The train chugs on.

entries.title: Made it to Kashgar!
entries.text:
47 hours later, we made it to the westernmost big city in Xinjiang!

Instantly headed to the hostel (apparently the only one in all of
Xinjiang), and SHOWERED.

On the taxi in, I spotted fresh naan and lamb skewers, and Matthew spotted
street vendors selling pomegranate and melon. We won't be going hungry here

Off to the streets!

entries.title: Train day 3
entries.text:
Freedom at last! 

As we stagger from our mobile cage the sun is brighter, the air carries the scents of soil and flowers, the birds overhead an orchestra. 

We emerge victorious. 

Today the land of Xinjiang passed our window in a blur. More fertile than the desolation of the Gansu corridor, with the exception of a small section that looked like Jordan, with cotton and pomegranate in bountiful quantities. We were told 20% of all the earths cotton is grown here and it is hard to doubt the claim looking out at the fields, with the occasional farmer hand picking their crop.

There were the most beautiful mountains today. The high peaks of the Kyrgyz border visible from our carriage and the multicoloured rainbow hills up against the tracks. Reds, pinks, orange, yellow, and green rock in strata. 
Aymon got some pics so maybe you’ll see them. 

The train is a fantastic experience and way to see the country. With the exception of the grannies throwing their wake up party loudly at 04:30 local time! The beds are more than long enough even for the usual westerner, I recommend them to anyone under 6 foot/180cm. The idea that there is hardship is limited to the confined space and quality of the food you brought, the staff swept regularly, everything was cleaned often, and the people are very kind and friendly. Indeed, we have amassed yet more tea as gifts, the joyful burden now well over 2 kg worth. 

Thank you all, enjoy any train you have the privilege to be on. Here comes Xinjiang

entries.title: Exploring Xinjiang
entries.text:
After 2 days in Kashgar, we've decided to check out the southern road on
the perimeter of the Taklamakan Desert.

Our experience so far in Xinjiang has been different to what we expected,
but just as fun.

What was aligned with our expectations:

• NAAN BREAD and YOGHURT!!! With naan and yoghurt, Matthew is happy. With
bbq lamb skewers, I am happy. Food has been ELITE
• Even the locals thinking that Matthew is Uyghur
• I am getting strong flashbacks to Kazakhstan. This all looks so different
to Chengdu and Guizhou

What surprised us:
• a "small" town in China may have very few western tourists, but thousands
of domestic Chinese tourists
• with that in mind, even the smallest towns have 3-5 cheap hotels that
international guests can stay at

---------

At our hostel in Kashgar, out of the 5 other guests we met not one, but TWO
Aussies!!
1. One of them was a 20 y/o down in the dumps after having a travel
relationship not turn out so good :( so we took him under our wing as we
explored Kashgar.
2. The other Aussie we might end up meeting up in Turpan in a few days!

Matthew and I debated sample bias, as we realised that everyone else in
this hostel had:

• travelled to Afghanistan
• is at least on a 6 month trip
• crazy stories (one dude kayaked some 300km river in Kazakhstan, another
guy is mountain biking through the snowy mountain passes, etc...)

Eventually, we moved on from Kashgar, and after a failed attempt at hitch-
hiking (the officials politely stopped the next bus for us), we are now in
the next town 2 hours east (Yarkant).

---------

Now what?

We're on the southern road, but eventually need to be on the north side of
the desert. From Hotan (next major city), there's a road that crosses the
ENTIRE desert and brings us back to the North side. 600km traverse.

It's unclear to us if there's much traffic on that road. Ideally we'll
hitch-hike through it, or get put on a bus.

If no traffic appears, we'll backtrack our steps to Kashgar and take our
originally "planned" route.

That's all for now, hopefully tomorrow you'll see pictures of us on camels!!

entries.title: Xinjiang Updates
entries.text:
Hello all, 

We’re on a train to the South Xinjiang city of Hotan after failing to hitchhike as the officials weren’t too keen. 

Aymon converted most of the last few days in his post I think (haven’t read it) but couldn’t upload photos. So here’s some photos! 
Kashgar was super cool made lots of local and international friends, though all the travellers were mad and had separately been to Afghanistan in the last few weeks for fun.

Wherever we are was also cool for two days and far less polished, people were astounded to see Aymon. Though I could be a stock image picture of a Uighur apparently as they all think I’m local. Kids in Xinjiang speak way more English than in the east. 

Stay safe out there!

entries.title: Cirque du Soleil, but Chinese
entries.text:
Unfortunately we have no camel photos to share just yet, but (after a
kerfuffle this morning) we have made it to Hetan!

As is now routine, we get a taxi to the highway toll booth, we get out, and
within 15 seconds we have traffic police come talk to us. This time they
seemed quite friendly, and (after much hesitation) actually asked a few
cars if they would take two such fine individuals on a 4 hour drive.

According to the officials, with all the checkpoints and controls, the
drivers they talked to weren't too keen on letting two random people in
their cars. Let alone two foreigners!!

Realistically, they only asked 2 cars, and we had plenty of vehicles slow
down and say hi as we walked back to the train station with our tails
between our legs.

Alas, we eventually got on the train and ended up meeting 2 other solo
chinese backpackers!

They suggested that we explore the old city with them. Apparently there was
an evening show at 8pm. We've seen these before, every "old city" (often
rebuilt in the last 10 years) seems to have some opening or closing
ceremony with traditional dances. So we weren't expecting anything crazy.

That could not have been further from the truth.

Imagine a MASSIVE complex, that looks just like a traditional desert town
from thousands of years ago. Like Disney, but with Chinese-scale
infrastructure. I cannot emphasise how MASSIVE and realistic it looked.

As you walk through, there's tonnes of actors and actresses in traditional
costume, singing, dancing, playing traditional instruments.

THEN, at 9pm sharp, all the lights go off and the actors rush you to the
main square, where a Cirque du Soleil style performance begins out of
nowhere.

I'm talking (real!) horses, flying dancers, fire, dragons flying through
the sky, and actors in every direction you can see. There's no "stage".
You're amongst all the actors. As they run off, you follow them through
this desert town.

(being the only foreigners there, we kept getting pulled in by the actors,
our two chinese friends found this quite hilarious)

What we thought was going to be a "regular" traditional dance, ended up
being a crazy immersive theatre experience. Good thing those two travellers
recommended that we joined them!!!

We then headed to the night market, avoiding the ridiculous number of
stalls selling either testicles or fish (despite being 2,000 km from the
nearest sea), and settled from some safe veggie fried rice.

Off to bed, finally on an actual mattress!

entries.title: Back on the train we go!
entries.text:
In today's episode of "you don't know what you've got till it's gone":
mattresses!

We slept 11 hours.

I'm sure the rock hard traditional Chinese mattress has sooooome health
benefits, and that soft mattresses are somehow ruining are backs.

Regardless, we hibernated last night and woke up reborn.

After checking out the quite disappointing "old-town", not so in-use mosque
and not so "grand" bazaar, we headed to the Jade market.

Hotan is to this day China's epicentre for jade!! Pretty impressive for a
super remote town of 300k people. We de ides to investigate the MASSIVE
market with at least 500 booths.

In the process, we picked up little pieces of rock somehow worth $10k usd
(and carefully placed them back down), before settling on little souvenirs
worth closer to $10. (pictured)

After deliberating between hitch-hiking across the desert highway, taking
the overnight bus, or getting on the brand new train line, we find
ourselves yet again at home in the hard sleeper train.

We'll be rolling into Turpan tomorrow morning, where we will hopefully meet
up with an Aussie mate we briefly met in Kashgar 10mins before leaving!

entries.title: Last stop in Xinjiang: Turpan
entries.text:
We yet again found ourselves waking up to the chugging of the train. This
time heading eastwards, parallel to the Taklamakan Desert.

This train was much bumpier and louder than the last, with way more twists
and turns in the track. Odd since this track was only built 3 years ago.

Matthew recalls waking up throughout the night to our bags falling off the
rack, and catapulting to the ground. It's unclear if he was dreaming or
that actually happened. Personally, I slept like a baby.

Anyway, we made our oats and arrived in Turpan mid-morning. After hearing
about this town from the Turpan basketball team (that won the finals back
in Taipan weeks ago) we had high hopes for this city.

We'd organised to meet this Aussie guy at the hostel. Considering he'd been
here for 2 days already, we presumed he had some ideas of where to go.
Instead, he was mostly preoccupied in regretting his decision of not
joining his mates who are currently driving around Iran.

Matthew and I quickly do some research and make a vague plan of sights to
see. It appears that all the cool sights are out of town (most of which
we'll be visiting tomorrow), and the town itself isn't much of interest.

We make our way towards what appears to be a lovely mosque on Amap (the
chinese version of Google maps). When we arrive at the location, we can't
see anything of resemblance. This isn't unusual. Amap is confusing at best,
and inaccurate at worst.

Hoping to get directions, we show the photo of the mosque to these guys
sitting across the street, who reply with "before".

They eventually explain that it had been removed last year, and is now
replaced by an apartment block...

After dilly dallying around this town with zero attractions, museums, or
much happening at all, we walk past this square full of life, with dozens
of table tennis tables and people playing badminton. We head around the
corner to buy some €3 bats.

Now equipped with the right tools, we end up spending our afternoon playing
table tennis and badmiton with the locals, with some traditional chinese
music in the background. Now this felt very Chinese.

Matthew has made it very clear to me that he is not leaving Xinjiang until
he has ridden a camel, so tomorrow we're renting a taxi for the day with a
German guy to find some (and also to see some of the real attractions of
this area).

Ciaooo

entries.title: Mango Pizza with Tibetan buddhist monks
entries.text:
After going east on the train for 18 hours, and a 4hr bus into the
mountains, we find ourselves in the buddhist town of Xiahe, home or Labrang
temple.

In the cafe directly outside our hotel we found 3 super chill monks, just
had the most interesting and random and fascinating conversation in a
loooooooong time. Will send through more info tomorrow as we undoubtedly
uncover more

Learnings so far:
- most of them eat meat
- they get paid a stipend from the Tibetan compatriots
- when we asked if/how often they visit Tibet, they replied with a 🤫🤫🤫
- apparently pink is an official robe colour too
- they seem to love pizza and coffee!!

entries.title: Unusual day in the monastery
entries.text:
Today was an unusual day, akin to a fever dream for each hour yielded a different pleasant surprise.

At sunrise we walked the hour long route around the compound spinning prayer wheels with the faithful, a very nice but early start. This was followed by a breakfast of the only true leavened bread we have seen since our journey to the Middle Kingdom began. Not so unusual a start.

Yet, out here in the remote Tibetan Plateau we found 18 Dutch over 65 year olds, many of whom wore shoes with individual toes, touring China for a month. We have not seen more than 2 Europeans at a time all month, so this was shocking to us, truly the Dutch are everywhere. After touring the monastery with them we split off and discovered in this small town, one of the 6 great monasteries of the sect of the Dali Lama, there is a huge mosque too! We walked in just as midday prayers were starting and watched proceedings, looked around, and exchanged signs of peace with the congregation. This constitutes the first active mosque we have found in China. A note worth pausing on.

After this we volunteered to help the old ladies of the village reenforce part of the mountain after large erosion and carried bags of dirt up and down the hill, they were surprised by both ourselves and the assistance. 

Finally we found ourselves in conversation with another perplexing monk who chatted about how much he loved the show Shameless and the Shawshank Redemption. Not really monk appropriate! Along with the fact they eat meat, love iPhones, and play lots of jokes on eachother it appears they are more playful and less serious than initially thought. The monk gifted me the pin from his university very kindly. 

Perhaps written the strangeness of each experience is lessened, but trust that from our perspective this was a curious day! 

Aymon has better pics, also yak butter smells really bad and as a result so do most of the offerings at temple. :/
